facts.value: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26 — full year outturn. Covering report (doc 47328) plus Appendix 1 the Annual Report itself (doc 47329) with §1-9 narrative and Annex 1 prudential indicators table. Both PDFs held on disk as extracted .raw.txt. Report to Audit & Standards Committee 29 June 2026, then Full Council 30 September 2026. Adviser Arlingclose Ltd throughout.

source.title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26 Covering Report + Appendix 1 Annual Report — Audit & Standards Committee, 29 June 2026

facts.note: Covering report (47328) is a five-page committee wrapper carrying no numbers. Appendix 1 (47329) carries every figure. The two were separately extracted; between them the paper is complete. Earlier session (14 August) held only 47328 and recorded 'no figures'; that is now superseded — 47329 is on disk and reconciles.

facts.value: Total Debt £8m at 31/03/26 at 5.4% average rate, average life 32.5 days (£0 at 31/03/25). Total Investments £4.05m at 31/03/26 at 1.76% snapshot yield, average life 1 day (£3.05m at 2.7% at 31/03/25).

source.title: Appendix 1 (47329) §3 Treasury Position as at 31 March 2026, p.3

facts.note: Paper notes verbatim that the £4.05m investment figure is only a snapshot and 'large fluctuations in cash inflows and outflows that occur throughout the month can have an impact on the figure reported'. The £8m debt / 32.5-day average life confirms this is short LA-to-LA or bank facility money, not PWLB — matches price_book.py --find (no borrower record).

facts.value: Average return 3.71% across the year on an average individual investment of £1.647m; actual interest income £0.231m. 88 investments in 2025/26, 87 of them for two weeks or less, none longer than 16 days. 8 investments with Public Sector Deposit Fund; 80 with the Debt Management Account Deposit Facility (DMADF). Also funds held on the general fund account at Lloyds Bank. No target set for 2025/26 as the strategy assumed a net interest payable position to fund the capital programme.
facts.note: 91% of the investment count sat at DMADF (HMG counterparty); the remainder at the CCLA Public Sector Deposit Fund — essentially zero credit risk across the entire operation. Snapshot yield 1.76% at 31/3/26 (§3) is well below the 3.71% year-average because 31 March is at the cash low point (grants received earlier in the year drove the £1.647m per-investment average).

facts.value: Annex 1 outturn: Capital Expenditure 25/26 A £27.348m (indicator £35.634m); CFR at 31/3/26 £21.807m (indicator £35.061m; 31/3/25 £19.893m); Borrowing £8m / OLL £0 / Total Debt £8m / Investments (£4.05m) / Net Borrowing £3.95m; Authorised Limit indicator £100m; Operational Boundary indicator £80m (actual maximum £8m); Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream 25/26 A (0.98%) [indicator 5.19%; 24/25 A (2.29%)]; Variable rate limits Loans 0-100% / Investments 0-100% (actual 0% / 0%); Actual External Debt £8m; Principal Funds Invested >365 days actual £0 against limit £25m.
facts.note: Financing cost ratio at (0.98%) is one of the rare negative readings in the batch — investment income still exceeded financing costs in 2025/26 even after taking on £8m of debt. Indicator had been set at 5.19% assuming heavier borrowing. CFR undershot indicator by £13.254m (£21.807 vs £35.061) because capital expenditure came in £8.286m below plan (£27.348 vs £35.634). Long-term investment permission of £25m in every year was £0 used.

facts.value:
CFR − external borrowing − other long-term liabilities = internal borrowing.
• 31/3/25 A:  19.893 − 0.000 − 0.000 = 19.893m  TIES
• 31/3/26 A:  21.807 − 8.000 − 0.000 = 13.807m  TIES

Movement year-on-year: CFR up £1.914m; external borrowing up £8.000m; internal borrowing down £6.086m. Interpretation: the £8m new external draw more than covered the £1.914m CFR growth, releasing £6.086m of internal resources back onto the balance sheet.
facts.note: Identity ties exactly at both year-ends. 63.3% of the 31/3/26 CFR is still funded internally (£13.807m of £21.807m); at 31/3/25 it was 100% internal. This is a council that has just begun terming out — the first £8m of external debt on the balance sheet after years of running debt-free.

facts.value: No PWLB borrower record for Newcastle-under-Lyme in price_book.py. Confirmed via price_book.py --find 'Newcastle-under-Lyme' (no match), --find 'Under Lyme' (no match), --find 'Lyme' (no match), --find 'Newcastle' (only NEWCASTLE ON CLUN PC and NEWCASTLE UPON TYNE CITY COUNCIL, both unrelated). The paper's own §3 shows Total Debt of £8m at a 32.5-day average life — the maturity profile of temporary LA-to-LA or bank-facility money rather than PWLB. Our zero holding is consistent with the paper.
facts.note: This is the reconciliation for a council with no PWLB debt: absence on both sides. Nothing to compare loan-count or rate against. Recorded as a clean tie — the alternative interpretation (that our file is missing PWLB loans that should be there) is contradicted by the 32.5-day average life on the paper's own table.

facts.value: Strategy approved by Council 12 February 2025. Authorised Limit £100m; Operational Boundary £80m; borrowing not normally to exceed Operational Boundary. Fixed/variable rate loans and investments both permitted 0-100%. Long-term investment permissions: £25m maturing beyond 31/3/26, £25m beyond 31/3/27, £25m beyond 31/3/28. Overriding consideration: safeguard capital; within that, maximise return.
facts.note: Both directions massively underutilised through the year: max debt used was £8m of an £80m Operational Boundary; long-term investments used were £0 of £25m. That is a treasury operation running very cautiously in both directions relative to the permissions Council granted. Minor typo: third line of the long-term investment permissions reads '25m' rather than '£25m'.

facts.value: Adviser narrative (Arlingclose): Bank Rate cut to 3.75% at December 2025 MPC; held 5-4 at 3.75% in February 2026 and unanimously in March. Markets had priced a cut to 3.50% at March before the US/Israel-Iran conflict at end February; conflict re-priced hikes back in. Arlingclose's revised central view post-March is Bank Rate held at 3.75%. Ten-year gilt: 4.65% start of year, 4.86% end, low 4.23% and high 4.95% in the space of a month. Twenty-year: 5.18% → 5.45%, low 4.92% / high 5.55%. SONIA averaged 4.01% over the 12 months to 31 March 2026.

officer.body:
Dear [RECIPIENT NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on your Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26, ahead of it landing at Full Council on 30 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report is clean and short, which we say plainly because most of what we read isn't, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

One thing worth stating up front, because it's the clearest cross-check we can offer for a paper like yours. We hold no PWLB loans for the Council in our book, and that matches your §3: your Total Debt walked from £0 to £8m across the year at a 32.5-day average life, which is short LA-to-LA or bank-facility money rather than PWLB. So both sides agree the Council holds no PWLB debt today. That saves any doubt about whether we're comparing like with like.

What did catch our eye is that £8m sitting at 5.4% in your §3, against the SONIA year-average of 4.01% your own §6 prints. That's roughly a 1.4 point spread over the shortest reference in the sterling market. Very short LA money did trade wide of SONIA through parts of 2025/26 — this isn't unusual — but it's the one testable rate on the paper against a reference the paper itself gives, and it's the sort of comparison our monthly sector page at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is built for. July's PWLB activity ran to £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% on the certainty rate, so the reference frame against which any short paper is priced does move month to month.

The other thing visible from Annex 1 is the shape of the balance sheet. Your CFR is £21.807m at 31 March, external borrowing £8m, no other long-term liabilities, so £13.807m — about 63% of the underlying capital financing requirement — is still funded internally from your own cash. A year earlier it was £19.893m and all of it internal. So this is a council that has just taken its first step into external debt while releasing about £6m of internal resources back onto the balance sheet, and it's done so with the Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream ratio still coming out at (0.98%) actual — investment income remaining ahead of financing cost after the draw. That's an unusual line to still see printing in brackets in 2026, and it's the sort of position the liability benchmark pathway is most useful for looking at ahead, because the whole conversation about when to term out is more open here than at most councils we've read.

Our quickest page to look at is pwlbtoday.org — daily PWLB rates at both fixings, the SONIA path, and the monthly sector activity all sit on the front. Nothing on it requires a subscription and nothing turns into a sales call.

On training, three fit the paper. PWLB rates — reading the curve is the natural companion to §5 and §6 of your report. Short-term liquidity and the LA-to-LA market is where the 5.4% at 32.5-days conversation sits. And the Liability benchmark pathway is worth a look given CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151, and given the internal-borrowing question your Annex 1 quietly opens. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are open to the whole team.

And if any of it turns out to be useful, mentioning it to colleagues or neighbours would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
